title: The silence and gentleness of Jesus
source_text: Ἐπεὶ δέ φησι μετὰ τὸν κατάλογον τῶν τοσούτων ἀνδρῶν τό· τί τοιοῦτον ὁ ὑμέτερος θεὸς κολαζόμενος ἐφθέγξατο; εἴποιμεν ἂν πρὸς αὐτὸν ὅτι παρὰ ταῖς μάστιξι καὶ ταῖς πολλαῖς αἰκίαις αὐτοῦ σιωπῇ παντὸς τοῦ ἐν Ἕλλησιν ἐν περιστάσεσι τυγχάνοντος φθεγξαμένου μᾶλλον ἐνέφηνε καρτερίαν καὶ ὑπομονήν· εἴ γε κἂν τούτῳ πιστεύειν ὁ Κέλσος βούλεται εὐγνωμόνως ἀναγεγραμμένῳ ὑπὸ φιλαλήθων ἀνδρῶν, τῶν καὶ τὰ παράδοξα ἀψευδῶς εἰρηκότων καὶ τὴν παρὰ ταῖς μάστιξι σιωπὴν αὐτοῦ ἐκείνοις συναριθμησάντων. ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐμπαιζόμενος καὶ ἐνδυόμενος τὴν „κοκκίνην χλαμύδα“ καὶ τὸν „ἀκάνθινον στέφανον“ τῇ κεφαλῇ περιτιθέμενος καὶ τὸν „κάλαμον“ λαμβάνων ἐπὶ τῆς χειρὸς ἀντὶ σκήπτρου ἄκρᾳ πρᾳότητι ἐχρήσατο, μηδὲν μηδ᾿ ἀγενὲς μηδ᾿ ἀγανακτητικὸν εἰπὼν πρὸς αὐτοὺς, τοσαῦτα κατ᾿ αὐτοῦ τολμήσαντας. οὐκ ἦν οὖν κατὰ τὸν ἀπὸ καρτερίας παρὰ ταῖς μάστιξι σιωπήσαντα καὶ ἀπὸ πρᾳότητος πάντα ὑπομένοντα τὰ παρὰ τῶν ἐμπαιζόντων προσαγόμενα εἰρηκέναι ἀπὸ ἀγεννείας, ὡς οἴονταί τινες, καὶ τό· „πάτερ, εἰ δυνατὸν, τὸ ποτήριον παρελθέτω τοῦτο ἀπ᾿ ἐμοῦ· πλὴν οὐχ ὡς ἐγὼ θέλω, ἀλλ᾿ ὡς σύ.“ ἔχει μὲν οὖν λόγον ἡ δοκοῦσα ὑποπαραίτησις εἶναι τοῦ καλουμένου ποτηρίου, ὃν ἐν ἄλλοις ἐπὶ πλεῖον ἐξητάσαμεν καὶ ἀποδεδώκαμεν. ἵνα δ᾿ ἁπλούστερον ἀκούσωμεν τοῦ λελεγμένου. ὅρα εἰ μὴ μετὰ τῆς πρὸς τὸν θεὸν εὐσεβείας καὶ ἡ εὐχὴ εἴρηται, παντὸς οὑτινοσοῦν τὸ περιστατικὸν οὐ προηγούμενον εἶναι νομίζοντος, ἀλλ᾿ ὑπομένοντος τὸ μὴ προηγουμένως συμβαῖνον, ὅταν καιρὸς καλῇ. ἀλλὰ καὶ οὐκ ἐνδεδωκότος ην ἡ φωνὴ, εὐαρεστουμένου δὲ τοῖς συμβαίνουσι καὶ προτιμῶντος τὰ ἀπὸ προνοίας περιστατικὰ ἡ λέγουσα φωνή· „πλὴν οὐ τί ἐγὼ θέλω, ἀλλὰ τί σύ.“
pass_a_gloss: And since after the catalogue (κατάλογος) of so many men he says: 'what such did your god utter being punished?', we would say to him that at the scourges (μάστιγες) and his many outrages (αἰκίαι), by silence (σιωπή), more than every one among the Greeks who uttered [something] when in circumstances (περιστάσεις), he displayed (ἐμφαίνω) endurance (καρτερία) and patience (ὑπομονή); if indeed Celsus wishes to believe this too, recorded (ἀναγράφω) in good faith (εὐγνωμόνως) by truth-loving (φιλαλήθης) men, who also spoke the marvellous things (παράδοξα) without falsehood (ἀψευδῶς) and counted with them (συναριθμέω) his silence at the scourges. But also being mocked (ἐμπαίζω) and putting on (ἐνδύομαι) the 'scarlet (κόκκινος) cloak (χλαμύς)' and having the 'thorny (ἀκάνθινος) crown' put around (περιτίθημι) the head and taking the 'reed (κάλαμος)' on the hand instead of a sceptre (σκῆπτρον), he used utmost (ἄκρος) gentleness (πρᾳότης), saying nothing either ignoble (ἀγενής) or resentful (ἀγανακτητικός) to them, who dared (τολμάω) so much against him. It was not then fitting for the one who from endurance was silent at the scourges and from gentleness endured (ὑπομένω) all the things brought (προσάγω) by the mockers to have said from ignobility (ἀγέννεια), as some think, also this: 'Father, if possible, let this cup (ποτήριον) pass by (παρέρχομαι) from me; yet not as I will (θέλω), but as you.' The seeming (δοκέω) request to be excused (ὑποπαραίτησις) from the so-called cup has a rationale (λόγος), which elsewhere we examined (ἐξετάζω) more fully and rendered (ἀποδίδωμι). But that we may hear more simply (ἁπλούστερον) what was said, see whether the prayer (εὐχή) was not also said with piety (εὐσέβεια) toward God, everyone whosoever (οὑτινοσοῦν) thinking the circumstantial (τὸ περιστατικόν) not to be preferred (προηγούμενον), but enduring what does not happen preferentially (προηγουμένως), whenever the occasion (καιρός) calls. But also the voice was not of one who had given in (ἐνδίδωμι), but of one well pleased (εὐαρεστέομαι) with what happens and preferring (προτιμάω) the circumstances from providence (πρόνοια), the voice saying: 'yet not what I will, but what you [will].'
pass_b_english: And since, after his list of so many men, he says, “What did your God say that was like this, while he was being punished?”, we would say to him that by his silence under the scourges and his many torments (Matthew 27:12–14) Jesus showed more endurance and patience than any Greek who spoke out under hardship; if, that is, Celsus is willing to believe even this, recorded in good faith by men who loved the truth, who told even the marvels without falsehood and counted among them his silence under the scourges.

Moreover, when he was mocked, and dressed in the “scarlet cloak”, and the “crown of thorns” was set about his head, and he took the “reed” in his hand in place of a sceptre (Matthew 27:28–29; John 19:5), he showed the utmost gentleness, saying nothing ignoble or resentful to those who dared so much against him. It was not, then, in keeping with one who kept silent under the scourges out of endurance, and who bore with gentleness everything that his mockers brought upon him, to have said out of cowardice, as some think, the words: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; yet not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39).

What seems to be a plea to be spared the cup, as it is called, has indeed its own explanation, which we have examined and set out at greater length elsewhere. But to take the saying more simply, see whether the prayer too was not spoken with piety toward God. For everyone at all regards hardship as not a matter of first choice, and yet, when the occasion calls, endures what does not come about by first choice. Moreover, the voice that says, “Yet not what I will, but what you will” (Mark 14:36), was not the voice of one who had given way, but of one well content with what was happening, and who put first the hardships sent by providence.

choices.choice: Celsus’s question repeats 7.53. The Gospels record Jesus’s silence before the high priest, Pilate and Herod (Matthew 26:63; 27:12–14; Mark 15:5; Luke 23:9), but not expressly under the scourging; Origen draws the silence from the narrative as a whole, so the inline reference points to the nearest passage. ‘Jesus’ is supplied as subject in English for clarity. ‘Scarlet cloak’ follows Matthew 27:28 (χλαμύδα κοκκίνην); ‘crown of thorns’ uses John’s ἀκάνθινον στέφανον (John 19:5; Matthew 27:29 has στέφανον ἐξ ἀκανθῶν); the reed in the right hand is Matthew 27:29. Origen’s form of Matthew 26:39 lacks μου and has the order τὸ ποτήριον παρελθέτω τοῦτο. The closing words follow Mark 14:36 (οὐ τί ἐγὼ θέλω ἀλλὰ τί σύ). ‘Elsewhere’ (ἐν ἄλλοις) is not identified; a lost commentary or the Exhortation to Martyrdom (29) is possible. τὸ περιστατικὸν οὐ προηγούμενον and τὸ μὴ προηγουμένως συμβαῖνον use Stoic terms for what is ‘preferred’ and for ‘circumstances’ of hardship; rendered in plain English. ἀγέννεια rendered ‘cowardice’ (lack of nobility). The awkward ἀλλὰ καὶ οὐκ ἐνδεδωκότος ἦν ἡ φωνὴ ... ἡ λέγουσα φωνή is restructured with the quotation moved forward, without change of sense. Review: ἔχει λόγον rendered ‘has its own explanation’ (the earlier ‘deeper meaning’ added ‘deeper’); ὃν refers back to this λόγος. The genitive absolute παντὸς ... νομίζοντος ... ὑπομένοντος is rendered positively (‘everyone regards ... and yet endures’) to keep the Greek negation exactly. ἀλλὰ καί at the last sentence rendered ‘Moreover’. προτιμῶντος rendered ‘put first’, matching ‘first choice’ for προηγούμενον.
ἐν περιστάσεσι: cliché 'in his hour of trial' -> 'under hardship'
ἔχει λόγον: 'a deeper meaning' (addition) -> 'its own explanation'; ἀποδεδώκαμεν 'explained' -> 'set out'
genitive absolute on hardship and first choice recast in natural order with exact negation

choices.choice: 7.55: the inline citation for Jesus's silence 'under the scourges' (Matthew 27:12–14) points to his silence before Pilate; no Gospel puts the silence exactly at the scourging. The citation is kept, as the nearest passage, and the note says so. Owner may prefer to drop it.
